title: The Metadata Nobody Sees
subtitle: I did the logging work by hand, then built the n8n pipeline that turns sermon videos into source-linked material for an AI product
team: Solo product, design and development; grounded with the logging team

sections.headline: The Metadata Nobody Sees
sections.subtext: Most sermon videos arrived with no structured way for the product to know which passage was discussed, where the useful segment began, or why it answered a question. I first did the logging work by hand, then built the n8n pipeline that turns timed transcripts into source-linked clips, chapters and retrievable material.

sections.headline: A correct search result could still look wrong
sections.content:
Bibel TV's catalogue contains sermons, Bible studies and lectures. Connecting that catalogue to a Bible-study product requires more than a transcript. The system needs to know which passage is discussed, when the discussion starts and ends, and what the segment is about.

The failure became concrete in one result. A sermon titled **"Who is Jesus?"** also discussed the creation account. Someone reading that passage could receive a technically relevant result whose inherited video title made it look irrelevant. The search had found the right source and still failed to explain itself.

A timestamp was not merely metadata. It was a product interface: the address a person would tap, the point where playback would begin, and the boundary of the evidence supporting an answer.

sections.headline: I learned the workflow before automating it
sections.content:
During onboarding I spent a week with the logging team and did the capture work on real videos. Scripture extraction alone took three to five minutes per video by my own count, sometimes more. The broader task also included identifying structure, recording timecodes, capturing graphics and selecting a cover frame.

That experience shaped the automation boundary. The goal was not to make a model watch a video so a person never had to. It was to remove repeated capture work and make the resulting structure usable by a product. I built a feasibility prototype first, then carried its validated transcript-driven extraction approach into the Bible-study app's active product pipeline.

sections.headline: Turn the transcript into product structure

steps.label: Create one consistent transcript
steps.description: The n8n transcription workflow obtains the source video, extracts audio and stores timed transcript segments in Postgres. The app's own catalogue status is the source of truth instead of accepting transcripts of unknown provenance.

steps.label: Derive clips, chapters and topics
steps.description: A second active workflow converts the timed transcript into Bible-passage clips and structural chapters. Clip text is derived deterministically from source segments rather than invented by the model.

steps.label: Make each segment retrievable
steps.description: The workflow creates embeddings and structured records that connect each virtual clip back to its source video and time range. The app can retrieve the segment as evidence for a Bible-study answer.

steps.label: Keep cost and failure visible
steps.description: Model usage and estimated cost are recorded with the corpus data. Live n8n traces exposed an execution-order race and a broken upstream node reference; I fixed both and re-verified the transcription path end to end.

sections.headline: 805 source-linked clips were already serving the chat

metrics.label: Corpus snapshot
metrics.value: 805 sermon clips from 299 transcribed videos, checked live on 16 September 2026

metrics.label: Product connection
metrics.value: The clips were wired into the app's running chat system during development

metrics.label: Verified workflow
metrics.value: The corrected transcription path completed end to end; the sermon-insight workflow later passed a 31-node dry run on a real transcript

sections.narrative: This is a pipeline result, not an adoption metric. The app remains in development. What is already real is the path from a source video to retrievable, time-bounded material that the product can cite, and the operational evidence behind it.

sections.headline: Lower the floor without hiding the system
sections.content:
The useful automation is not the one that produces the most content. It is the one that makes its source, boundary and failure state legible. A virtual clip has a source video, a time range and text derived from the same timed segments. When the workflow fails, its state and cost remain inspectable.

That is the same interaction principle I use in configurable products: let AI remove the blank page and repetitive capture, then give the next person something they can inspect, correct and own.

sections.headline: The details worth discussing
sections.content: Curious why I removed an apparently useful legacy chain from the critical path, what two live execution failures taught me about n8n's branch behaviour, or why a clip title matters to retrieval quality? Get in touch.

executive.summary: Built a live-tested n8n pipeline that turns sermon videos into source-linked clips and retrievable material for an AI product, after first doing the logging work by hand.
executive.angle: Workflow productisation grounded in the manual work and hardened through live execution
